name: Thatcherism
summary: The political and economic approach of Margaret Thatcher's governments (1979-90): sound money and monetarism, tax cuts, privatisation, curbs on trade unions, wider home and share ownership, and a rolled-back state in the economy but a strong state in law, order and defence. It pairs free-market economics with traditional morals, national sovereignty and Euroscepticism.
scope: The Thatcher-era program, drawn from the 1979 Conservative manifesto, Thatcher's Bruges speech and Wikipedia accounts of her policies and Gamble's 'free economy and the strong state' summary. Later Conservative leaders and post-Thatcher neoliberalism are excluded; the pre-1979 manifesto was cautious on privatisation and unions, which later grew into flagship policies.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The manifesto says significant increases in defence spending will be necessary and promises better pay and conditions for the armed forces.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The manifesto says Britain needs strong, efficient police forces with high morale.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The manifesto says cutting government spending and borrowing is vital to controlling inflation.

central-planning.rationale: The Bruges speech says the economic history of the 1970s and 80s shows that central planning and detailed control do not work and that a State-controlled economy is a recipe for low growth.

class-collaboration.rationale: The manifesto says that in bringing about recovery government and public, management and unions, employers and employees should all be on the same side with a common interest.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The manifesto blames the Labour-union 'social contract' exchanges of promises for the road to ruin and seeks responsible pay bargaining by those at the bargaining table, not state-brokered deals.

direct-action.rationale: The manifesto says picketing violence and intimidation have gone much too far and sets its task as upholding Parliament and the rule of law.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Bruges speech credits NATO with the peace kept over 40 years and says each member of the Alliance must shoulder a fair share.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The manifesto says the rights of all British citizens legally settled here are equal before the law whatever their race, colour or creed; it states this for citizens, not for all people.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The manifesto's task is to restore incentives so that hard work pays and success is rewarded.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The manifesto promotes bringing North Sea oil and gas ashore as a source of national wealth.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The manifesto sought a proper contribution from nuclear power to energy supply.

free-trade.rationale: The Bruges speech sets as a guiding principle that Europe should not be protectionist and warns against greater external protection.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The manifesto stresses the importance of ensuring the continuing effectiveness of Britain's nuclear deterrent.

limit-growth.rationale: The manifesto sets lower taxes and restored incentives to encourage economic growth as the aim of its economic policy, with no environmental limit on growth.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Bruges speech says central planning and detailed control do not work, that personal endeavour does, and that free enterprise within a framework of law brings better results.

moral-incentives.rationale: The manifesto's task is to restore incentives so that hard work pays and success is rewarded.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Sermon says the Christian religion is a fundamental part of the national heritage, that the overwhelming majority wish it preserved and fostered, and that political structures alone are not enough.

national-church-status.rationale: The Sermon says the historic connection between Church and State in the laws of Scotland and England gives symbolic expression to the truth that the Christian religion is a fundamental part of the national heritage, which should be preserved.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The Bruges speech says the democratic model of a free enterprise society has proved itself superior to the State-controlled economy.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The manifesto keeps the National Health Service, decentralised rather than cut, and welfare for the old, sick and disabled, so it does not limit the state to protection from violence.

one-party-rule.rationale: The manifesto's stated tasks include upholding Parliament and the rule of law, and it calls Britain the inheritor of a long tradition of parliamentary democracy.

open-borders.rationale: The manifesto's quota system covering all entry for settlement and its pledge of firm action against illegal immigrants contradict open borders.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The manifesto lists the supremacy of Parliament and says its tasks include upholding Parliament and the rule of law.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The Bruges speech says willing cooperation between independent sovereign states is the best way to build Europe and that frontiers rolled back in Britain must not be re-imposed by a European super-state.

population-transfer.rationale: The manifesto says there can be no question of compulsory repatriation of immigrants.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The manifesto says price controls have done nothing to prevent inflation.

production-for-use.rationale: The manifesto says profits are the foundation of a free enterprise economy and that price controls can keep them from reaching an adequate level.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The manifesto says profits are the foundation of a free enterprise economy and that government and public, management and unions, employers and employees all share a common interest in raising profits.

public-ownership.rationale: The manifesto says more nationalisation would impoverish us and undermine freedom, and promises to sell back the aerospace and shipbuilding concerns and the National Freight Corporation shares.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The manifesto says the rights of all British citizens legally settled here are equal before the law whatever their race, colour or creed.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The manifesto says firm immigration control is essential and promises to severely restrict work permits, end settlement for temporary visitors and introduce a quota system for all entry for settlement.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Bruges speech says the aim should not be more detailed regulation from the centre but to deregulate and remove constraints on trade.

rehabilitation.rationale: The manifesto promises a tougher regime as a short, sharp shock for young criminals in certain detention centres, and more compulsory attendance centres.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: The manifesto promises council and new town tenants the legal right to buy their homes in the first session of the next Parliament.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The manifesto favours a National Heritage Fund and a maintenance fund for heritage property.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Sermon defends the historic connection expressed in law between Church and State in both Scotland and England as giving symbolic expression to a crucial truth.

separated-powers.rationale: The manifesto says a strong Second Chamber is necessary to revise legislation and to guarantee the constitution and liberties.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The manifesto says its task is to uphold Parliament and the rule of law and speaks of a growing disrespect for the rule of law.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The manifesto restricts the National Enterprise Board to administering temporary shareholdings to be sold, and the Bruges speech holds that central planning and detailed control do not work.

state-harmful.rationale: Britannica gives a limited role for government, not its abolition, as the doctrine's aim, and the manifesto's tasks include upholding Parliament and the rule of law.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The Bruges speech says Europe must maintain a sure defence through NATO and must strive to maintain the United States' commitment to Europe's defence.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Bruges speech sets as a guiding principle that the Community should not be protectionist.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The manifesto rejects a wealth tax and promises to deal with the most damaging features of the Capital Transfer and Capital Gains Taxes.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The manifesto says the top rate of income tax should be cut to the European average and rejects Labour's wealth tax.

total-state.rationale: Britannica gives limited government as the doctrine's aim, and the manifesto restricts state bodies such as the National Enterprise Board and says participation systems should not be imposed by law.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The 1979 manifesto says it is not the intention to reduce spending on the Health Service and promises to simplify and decentralise it, while allowing private pay-beds alongside.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Under the heading of a property-owning democracy the manifesto says it wants more people to have the security of owning property, through council house sales and employee share-ownership.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The manifesto says the rules about the unemployed accepting available jobs will be reinforced.

workers-councils.rationale: The manifesto commits to uphold Parliament and the rule of law and says it would be wrong to impose by law a system of worker participation in every company.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The manifesto welcomes closer involvement of workers in decisions at their workplace but says it would be wrong to impose by law a system of participation in every company.

missingStatements.text: Council tenants should have a legal right to buy their homes.
missingStatements.rationale: The right to buy was a headline 1979 pledge, central to the aim of a property-owning democracy.

missingStatements.text: The law should restrict strikes and picketing, for example by requiring secret ballots.
missingStatements.rationale: Limiting picketing, closed shops and strike funding was among the three changes to be made at once in 1979.

notes: Later pass 2026-11-17 (rules 7). Rebuilt on primary texts read in full: the 1979 manifesto, the Bruges speech, the Woman's Own and Sunday Times interviews and the 1988 Church of Scotland speech, with Britannica and Gamble's chapter as defining scholarship; answers that rested only on Wikipedia summaries or on inference were nulled with their history kept. Themes searched in these sources: economy, tax, unions, nationalisation, immigration, law and order, defence, Europe, family, health, constitution, religion and church-state. Themes with no stated position in them (abortion, gender, environment beyond energy, courts, most of world and liberty) stay null; Thatcher's Commons speeches (Hansard corpus), statute texts and the Foundation's other speeches would be the next sources. One Nation and later Thatcherites would answer some social questions differently.
